title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions
notes:
## 1. Topic Introduction — What Survives a Crash

Every collision conserves momentum; only some conserve kinetic energy. The classification — elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic — decides how the bodies separate, and powers billiards, crash engineering and particle detectors.

## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2020)

| Type | Momentum | Kinetic energy | Separation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Elastic** | Conserved | Conserved | Bodies separate | Billiard balls, gas molecules, atomic collisions |
| **Inelastic** | Conserved | Partly lost (heat, sound, deformation) | Bodies separate | Most real collisions; a dropped ball that bounces lower |
| **Perfectly inelastic** | Conserved | Maximum possible KE loss | Bodies **stick together** | Bullet embedding in a block; clay lumps |

**Momentum is conserved in all three** (isolated system); kinetic energy only in the first.

### 2.1 Elastic collision in one dimension

For masses $m_1, m_2$ with initial velocities $u_1, u_2$ (m_2 at rest is the standard case), solving momentum and KE conservation together gives:

$$v_1 = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \qquad v_2 = \frac{(m_1 - m_2)u_2 + 2m_1u_1}{m_1 + m_2}$$

With $m_2$ initially at rest ($u_2 = 0$):
$$v_1 = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}u_1, \qquad v_2 = \frac{2m_1}{m_1 + m_2}u_1$$

**Special cases (u₂ = 0):**
| Masses | Result |
|---|---|
| $m_1 = m_2$ | Velocities **exchange**: $v_1 = 0$, $v_2 = u_1$ |
| $m_1 \gg m_2$ | $m_1$ continues nearly unchanged; $m_2$ shoots off at ≈ $2u_1$ |
| $m_1 \ll m_2$ | $m_1$ **rebounds** at ≈ $-u_1$; $m_2$ barely moves |

### 2.2 Perfectly inelastic collision

Bodies stick: common final velocity $v = \dfrac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2}{m_1 + m_2}$.
KE lost = initial KE − final KE — the maximum possible consistent with momentum conservation.

**Worked numerical (4m, 2022):** A bullet of mass 0.02 kg moving at 500 m/s embeds in a block of mass 4.98 kg at rest. Find the velocity of the system and the kinetic energy lost.
$v = \dfrac{0.02 \times 500}{5.00} = 2$ m/s.
$KE_i = \frac{1}{2}(0.02)(500^2) = 2500$ J; $KE_f = \frac{1}{2}(5)(4) = 10$ J.
**KE lost = 2490 J (99.6%) — momentum kept, energy mostly gone.**

## 3. Conceptual Relationships

- **To Topics 11–12:** momentum conservation is the universal collision law; this topic adds the energy bookkeeping.
- **To Topic 20:** lost KE becomes heat — non-conservative dissipation inside the collision.
- **To Kinetic Theory (Unit 13):** gas molecules collide elastically — the model's foundation.
- **To real life:** car crumple zones maximise KE loss safely; neutron moderation in reactors exploits $m_1 = m_2$ velocity exchange (hydrogen moderators).

## 4. Exam Orientation and Previous Year Questions (NEB)

### 4.1 Verified PYQs from the solved-paper bank

| Year | Unit | Topic | Question | Marks | Type |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2076/2020 | Mechanics | Collisions | Differentiate between elastic and inelastic collisions. | 3 | Difference |
| 2078/2022 | Mechanics | Perfectly inelastic | A bullet of mass 0.02 kg moving with a velocity of 500 m/s is embedded in a block of mass 4.98 kg initially at rest on a smooth horizontal surface. Find the velocity of the block. | 4 | Numerical |

### 4.2 Model answers

**Q1 (3m, 2020):** In an **elastic collision** both total momentum and total kinetic energy are conserved and the bodies separate after impact — e.g. collisions between billiard balls or gas molecules. In an **inelastic collision** momentum is conserved but part of the kinetic energy converts to heat, sound or deformation, and the bodies may or may not separate — e.g. a ball bouncing to a lower height. In the limiting **perfectly inelastic** case the bodies stick together and move with a common velocity — e.g. a bullet embedding in a block — with the maximum possible loss of kinetic energy.

**Q2 (4m, 2022):** see worked numerical in §2.2 — common velocity 2 m/s; 2490 J of the original 2500 J becomes heat and deformation.

### 4.3 Common examination mistakes

1. Claiming momentum is conserved only in elastic collisions — it is conserved in **all** of them.
2. Using the elastic-collision formulas for a sticking collision.
3. Forgetting the sign of $v_1$ when $m_1 < m_2$ (the projectile rebounds).
4. Computing "energy lost" as $KE_i$ instead of $KE_i - KE_f$.
5. Ignoring that the final mass in embedding problems is the sum.

summary: Collisions divide by what survives. **Momentum is always conserved** in an isolated collision; **kinetic energy only in elastic ones**. Elastic collisions (billiard balls, gas molecules) obey $v_1 = \frac{(m_1-m_2)u_1 + 2m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ — with equal masses the velocities simply exchange, a light projectile rebounds off a heavy target, and a heavy one ploughs through sending the light target off at nearly double speed. Inelastic collisions lose part of the KE to heat, sound and deformation; in the **perfectly inelastic** limit the bodies stick and move at $v = \frac{m_1u_1 + m_2u_2}{m_1+m_2}$ — a 0.02 kg bullet embedding in a 4.98 kg block leaves the pair at 2 m/s, having converted 2490 J of its 2500 J into heat (NEB 2022).
specialNotes: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects do NOT lose ALL their kinetic energy — only the KE relative to the center of mass can be lost.
The coefficient of restitution e depends on the materials, not on the velocities of the colliding bodies.
In an elastic collision between equal masses where one is initially at rest, the masses exchange velocities.
Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions (elastic and inelastic) as long as no external force acts.
NEB collision problems: always check whether the collision is elastic (use both conservation laws) or inelastic (use only momentum conservation).

notes: **प्रत्यास्थ टक्कर (Elastic collision):** एउटी टक्कर जहाँ कुल संवेग (momentum) र कुल गतिज ऊर्जा (kinetic energy) दुवै संरक्षित रहन्छ। पिण्डहरू स्थायी विकृति बिना प्रतिघात गर्छन्, शब्द/ताप उत्पादन हुन्न। सापेक्ष वेगको पहुँच = सापेक्ष वेगको अलगाव: v₂ - v₁ = u₁ - u₂।

**अप्रत्यास्थ टक्कर (Inelastic collision):** एउटी टक्कर जहाँ संवेग संरक्षित हुन्छ तर गतिज ऊर्जा संरक्षित हुँदैन। केही गतिज ऊर्जा आन्तरिक ऊर्जामा (ताप, शब्द, विकृति) परिवर्तित हुन्छ। प्रत्यास्थता गुणांक e < 1।

**पूर्ण अप्रत्यास्थ टक्कर (Perfectly inelastic collision):** चरम अवस्था जहाँ टक्कर खाने पिण्डहरू टक्करपछि एकसाथ रहन्छन् र सामान्य वेगसँग चल्छन्। संवेग संरक्षित हुन्छ; गतिज ऊर्जाको नोक्सान अधिकतम (तर १००% होइन किनकि संवेग संरक्षित हुनुपर्छ)।
importantStatements: प्रत्यास्थ टक्करमा संवेग र गतिज ऊर्जा दुवै संरक्षित रहन्छ।
अप्रत्यास्थ टक्करमा संवेग मात्र संरक्षित हुन्छ, गतिज ऊर्जा हुँदैन।
प्रत्यास्थता गुणांक e = (अलगावको सापेक्ष वेग) / (पहुँचको सापेक्ष वेग)।
केन्द्रको द्रव्यमान फ्रेममा कुल संवेग शून्य हुन्छ — यो 2D टक्कर विश्लेषण सरल बनाउँछ।

notes: Collision (noun): an instance of objects striking together. Plural: collisions.
Elastic (adjective): able to resume shape after deformation; in physics, KE-conserving.
Inelastic (adjective): not elastic; in physics, KE not conserved.
Coefficient of restitution (noun phrase): ratio of separation speed to approach speed.
importantStatements: In physics, 'elastic' means kinetic energy is conserved, not just that objects bounce back.
The term 'perfectly inelastic' means maximum kinetic energy loss consistent with momentum conservation.

subtopics.name: What is conserved
points: Momentum is conserved in ALL collisions
Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions

subtopics.name: Elastic collision
points: Both momentum and kinetic energy conserved
Relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation
For equal masses in 1D, the bodies exchange velocities

subtopics.name: Perfectly inelastic collision
points: Bodies stick together and move with a common velocity
Maximum kinetic energy loss of any collision type

subtopics.name: Coefficient of restitution
points: e = 1 elastic, e = 0 perfectly inelastic, 0 < e < 1 partially elastic

subtopics.name: Frame of reference
points: In the centre-of-mass frame, an elastic collision simply reverses both velocities
This makes elastic collision problems far simpler
Inelastic collisions look asymmetric in the lab frame but symmetric in the CM frame
